div.p: Scheduling strategies for non-preemptive real-time tasks on uniprocessors typically attempt to derive necessary and sufficient schedulability conditions in order to guarantee the timely execution of tasks. However, evaluating all conditions to allow the optimal scheduling of non-preemptive tasks is intractable, and is prohibitively expensive to be applied online. Therefore, on-line approaches, which often do not allow the liberty of exhaustive enumeration of the solution space, tend to be sub-optimal and heuristic in nature. Hence, offline techniques are often preferred over on-line techniques for solving such problems. Among the existing off-line techniques, formal approaches are the preferred choice due to their ability to guarantee correctness and completeness. Using Supervisory Control Theory (SCT) of Timed Discrete Event Systems (TDESs) as the underlying formal approach, this work proposes an off-line optimal scheduler synthesis framework for non-preemptive sporadic real-time tasks on uniprocessors.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Safety-critical systems must ensure guaranteed temporal behavior under all operating conditions as deadline misses could result in loss of human life, huge financial loss, or damage to the environment. Given a set of tasks corresponding to safety-critical applications, successfully satisfying all task deadlines is ultimately a scheduling problem. Generally, tasks are classified as aperiodic, sporadic and periodic, based on their arrival pattern [1]. These tasks can be scheduled either preemptively or non-preemptively. In the later case, execution of a task cannot be interrupted until its completion. Here, we consider the non-preemptive scheduling of aperiodic and sporadic tasks on uniprocessor systems.

Heuristic strategies for scheduling non-preemptive aperiodic tasks are generally sub-optimal in nature. Such suboptimal strategies typically suffer from drawbacks such as: (i) Lack of predictability in guaranteeing timeliness leading to cases where a schedule which is actually feasible may be deemed to be infeasible by the scheduler, and (ii) Poor resource usage leading to increased design costs resulting from conservative resource provisioning. However, the general problem of the optimal scheduling of non-preemptive tasks is intractable and requires exhaustive enumeration of the entire solution space [1]. Such exhaustive enumeration methodologies incur exponential overheads, and therefore are prohibitively expensive to be applied on-line. Hence, there is a necessity for developing off-line exhaustive enumeration techniques to pre-compute optimal schedules at design time and use them during on-line execution. In order to ensure

the correctness and completeness of such an enumeration process, formal approaches are often preferred.

Many researchers have shown that off-line formal approaches such as SCT of TDESs can be used for the design of real-time schedulers. Here, SCT allows the costruction of supervisors (i.e., schedulers) for TDES based real-time system models, that are guaranteed to perform correctly against a set of specifications in terms of temporal criticality of the tasks as well as system capacity. Optimal uniprocessor scheduling of non-preemptive periodic tasks was presented in [2]. Janarthanan et al. developed a formal and unified procedure for the scheduling of periodic tasks preemptively as well as non-preemptively on uniprocessors [3]. In [6], Xi et al. extended the models presented in [2], [3] to handle nonpreemptive periodic tasks with multiple periods. They have also proposed a framework for priority-free, conditionallypreemptive real-time scheduling of periodic tasks in [7].

In [4], Park and Cho proposed a scheme to synthesize a preemptive scheduler for dynamically arriving sporadic tasks on uniprocessor systems. Later, Park and Yang extended preemptive scheduling procedure to allow the co-execution of periodic and sporadic tasks with mutually exclusive accessibility of shared resources [5]. However, the scheduler synthesized in [4], [5] does not model minimum inter-arrival times, which is necessary for the accurate characterization of sporadic tasks. To summarize, there is a lack of optimal approaches which consider the non-preemptive scheduling of real-time aperiodic as well as sporadic tasks on uniprocessors. The principal contributions of this paper are as follows:

• Development of TDES based execution and deadline specification models for non-preemptive, aperiodic tasks with known arrival times. Later, these models have been extended to handle dynamically arriving aperiodic tasks. • Based on the individual task execution and timing specification models for a set of aperiodic real-time tasks, a framework for generating a correct-by-construction non-blocking supervisor has been presented. • The proposed execution and deadline specification models have been extended to incorporate non-preemptive scheduling of dynamically arriving sporadic tasks.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section II introduces a background on SCT of Timed DESs. Section III presents the scheduler synthesis framework. Section IV illustrates the scheduler design mechanism using a simple motor network example. Finally, Section V concludes this paper.

div.head: II. SUPERVISORY CONTROL THEORY OF TIMED DESS

div.head: A. Aperiodic Tasks with Known Arrival Times
div.p: System Model: We consider a real-time system consisting of a set I (= {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ n }) of n (≥ 1) non-preemptive, aperiodic tasks to be scheduled on a uniprocessor. Formally, the task τ i to be scheduled is represented by a 3-tuple A i , E i , D i , where A i is the arrival time, E i is the execution time and D i is the relative deadline of τ i .

Assumptions: (1) Tasks are independent with no precedence constraints. (2) Tasks cannot suspend itself until it completes. (3) Only one task is allowed to execute on the uniprocessor at a time. (4) E i ≤ D i for all tasks in I.

div.p: State 0 is the initial state of T i and represents the state in which task τ i resides prior to the start of the system. Events in the self-loop Σ \ (Σ i ∪ {t}) may be characterized as follows: Since τ i has not yet arrived, the events that are associated with τ i (Σ i ) are excluded from Σ. To elaborate, the self-loop contains the events such as arrival, start of execution, and completion with respect to any other task (τ j ∈ I, j = i) in the system. Thus, Σ \ (Σ i ∪ {t}) does not impose any restriction on the execution of other tasks. State 0 is replicated A i times in order to measure the occurrence of A i ticks subsequent to system start.

After the occurrence of a i at A i th tick, T i reaches State 3 from State 2. Here, the scheduler takes a decision whether to immediately allocate the task τ i for execution on a processor or make it wait on the ready queue. The latter is indicated by the self-loop transition Σ \ Σ i at State 3. If the scheduler decides to start the execution of τ i , then it will enable the event s i to assign τ i for execution on the processor. According to Figure 1, if event s i occurs at State 3, then T i reaches State 4. At State 4, the self-loop transition Σ uc \{a i } ensures that only arrivals (barring that of τ i ) but not the execution of tasks other than τ i are allowed. This is because τ i has already started its non-preemptive execution on the processor. After the elapse of E i ticks from State 4, T i reaches State 6. Finally, the event c i which is used to mark the completion of τ i 's execution, takes T i to the marked state State 7. Now, T i continues to stay at State 7 without imposing any constraint on other tasks currently executing on the processor. It may be noted that τ i consumes exactly E i ticks from the start of its execution at State 4. However, τ i may miss its deadline based on the amount of time spent in the ready-queue at State 3. div.formula: A sequence s = s 1 a i s 2 c i s 3 ∈ L m (T i ), where s 1 , s 3 ∈ Σ * , s 2 ∈ (Σ \ {c i }) * is deadline-meeting, if tickcount(s 2 ) ≤ D i . Otherwise, s is a deadline-missing sequence.

div.head: D. Supervisor Synthesis
div.p: In order to find all deadline-meeting sequences from L m (T ), we construct the finite state automaton M = T ×H. Theorem 1: L m (M ) contains only and all the deadlinemeeting sequences of L m (T ). Proof: We know that L m (T ) contains both deadline-meeting as well as deadline-missing sequences of all tasks in I (Remark 1(i)). On the other hand, L m (H) contains all possible deadline-meeting sequences (Remark 2(i)). Since L m (M ) = L m (T ) ∩ L m (H), L m (M ) contains only and all the deadline-meeting sequences of L m (T ).

Apart from the removal of deadline-missing sequences in L m (T ), the product composition also eliminates the sequences in L m (H) that violate Assumption 3. Although L m (M ) is deadline-meeting, the deadline-missing sequences in T lead to deadlock states in M , i.e., M is blocking. Hence, we apply safe state synthesis mechanism presented in Algorithm 1 to remove the minimal number of states from M until it becomes both controllable and non-blocking [9].
Remark 3: It may happen that Q s is an empty set implying that the given task set is non-schedulable.

div.head: E. Handling Arbitrary Aperiodic Task Arrivals
F. Handling Dynamically Arriving Sporadic Tasks
div.p: Let us consider a dynamically arriving sporadic task τ i E i , D i , P i , where E i is the execution time, D i is the deadline and P i is the minimum inter-arrival time. Here, we assume D i = P i , i.e., deadlines are implicit. The sporadic task τ i consists of an infinite sequence of identical instances that are separated by a minimum inter-arrival time P i [1].

Task execution model T i : In case of aperiodic tasks, we have considered the scheduling of a single instance. However, sporadic tasks consist of an infinite sequence of identical instances. Presently, T i shown in Figure 6(a) moves to State 5 from State 4 after the completion of a single instance of τ i and stays their indefinitely. This must be modified to support the execution of sporadic tasks. Figure 7(a) shows the modified T i corresponding to the dynamically arriving sporadic task τ i . Here, we have introduced a loopback to the initial state (State 0) from State 4 on completion event c i such that the execution of infinite sequences can be supported. In addition to this, we set State 0 as initial as well as marked state which implies that T i stays at State 0 prior to the arrival of next instance of τ i as well as after the completion of its current instance.

Remark 4: L m (T i ) includes (i) deadline-meeting, (ii) deadline-missing, (iii) sporadic and (iv) non-sporadic execution sequences for all tasks in I. All these sequences satisfy Assumption 3 (similar to Remark-1(ii)).

The different types of sequences in L m (T i ) (as specified in Remark 4) are also carry forwarded to L m (T ). In order to remove the sequences that violate the deadlines and / or sporadicity from L m (T ), we construct the timing specification model which captures the following aspects of a sporadic task, (i) infinite sequence of identical instances, (ii) minimum inter-arrival time and (iii) deadline satisfaction.

Timing specification model H i : Figure 7(b) shows the timing specification of a dynamically arriving, implicit deadline meeting sporadic task τ i . This model includes the set of states {8, 9, ..., 10} in addition to the states that are already present in H i (shown in Figure 6(b)) to capture the minimum inter-arrival time constraint. In order to model the infinite sequence of identical instances, a loop-back on completion event c i (from states {4, 5, ..., 6}) to the initial state (State 0) of H i have been added via states {8, 9, ..., 10}. Now, we explain how these newly added states take care of minimum inter-arrival time. Suppose, τ i executes c i , the completion event, P i -j ticks (j = {1, 2, ..., (E i -1)}) subsequent to its arrival. Then, it will reach anyone (say, State x) among the states 8, 9, ..., 10, such that all substrings between State x and State 0 contain j ticks. The self-loop Σ \ (Σ i ∪ {t}) at these states ({8, 9, ..., 10}) disallows the arrival of sporadic task τ i 's next instance before the elapse of P i ticks from the arrival of its current instance. Apart from this, the remaining states ({0, 1, ..., 7}) are same as H i (shown in Figure 6(b)), and hence L m (H i ) contains the deadline-meeting sequences. So, L m (H i ) satisfies the three aspects of a sporadic task.
Remark 5: L m (H i ) includes all and only the deadlinemeeting as well as sporadic execution sequences. However, these sequences may violate Assumption 3.

div.head: IV. APPLICATION EXAMPLE
div.p: We consider a simple motor network example (adopted from [2]) to illustrate the scheduler synthesis mechanism for a set of dynamically arriving sporadic tasks. Consider two electric motors whose speed stabilization is controlled by a real-time controller implemented on a uniprocessor as illustrated in Figure 8(a). The controller consists of two independent sporadic tasks τ 1 and τ 2 to control Motor 1 and Motor 2, respectively. While τ 1 requires 1 ms to stabilize Motor 1, τ 2 requires 2 ms for the same corresponding to Motor 2. Once stabilized, Motor 1 remains within its maximum destabilization threshold for at least 6 ms, while Motor 2 may destabilize after 3 ms subsequent to control action by τ 2 . τ 1 and τ 2 are invoked whenever motors 1 and 2 destabilize beyond their threshold limits. Thus τ 1 and τ 2 may be represented as τ 1 1, 6, 6 and τ 2 2, 3, 3 . Fig. 9: The supervisor S for motor network.

After obtaining T and H, they are product composed to obtain M whose marked behavior contains the set of sporadic and deadline-meeting sequences satisfying Assumption 3. Then, we apply Algorithm 1 to obtain the final non-blocking supervisor S (Figure 9) which contains all feasible schedules of the dynamically arriving sporadic tasks τ 1 and τ 2 .

div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we have presented a systematic way of synthesizing an optimal scheduler for real-time uniprocessor systems which process non-preemptive aperiodic and sporadic tasks. First, we have presented a scheduler synthesis mechanism for aperiodic tasks with known arrival times. Then, we have extended our scheme to incorporate dynamically arriving aperiodic tasks. Finally, we have presented the synthesis approach that considers dynamically arriving sporadic tasks. We have illustrated the practical applicability of our framework using a motor network example.
